clue.text: Where churchwardens may stand out?

blocks.note: surface reading: a spot where parish officials might be conspicuous, or stand outdoors
setter's reading: a churchwarden is also a long-stemmed clay tobacco pipe, which needs somewhere to be stood when not smoked

explanation.surface: Parish officials looking for a place where they will be noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: A churchwarden is a long clay pipe as well as a parish officer, and pipes are kept upright in a stand.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand holding tobacco pipes upright is exactly where long clay pipes would be kept on display.

clue.text: Old shell containing ammunition for shooters?

definitions.text: Old shell containing ammunition for shooters?

blocks.clueFragment: Old shell containing ammunition for shooters?
blocks.note: surface reading: an antique artillery shell still loaded with its charge
setter's reading: the seeds that children fire from peashooters, held inside an archaic word for their pod

explanation.surface: A vintage explosive shell found still packed with its charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' signals an archaic word, and 'shooters' are the toy tubes children blow dried seeds through.
explanation.definitionFit: Peascod is an old word for a pea pod, the green husk holding the seeds a peashooter fires.

clue.text: He takes his course from the bar at noon

definitions.text: He takes his course from the bar at noon

blocks.clueFragment: He takes his course from the bar at noon
blocks.note: surface reading: a pub-goer ordering a course of food over the counter at lunchtime
setter's reading: a farm worker drives straight furrows across a field, and the pub lunch of bread and cheese bears his name

explanation.surface: A man ordering lunch over the counter of a pub at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: A ploughman's lunch is a British pub meal of bread, cheese and pickle; the furrow he cuts is his course.
explanation.definitionFit: A farm labourer who works the land with a plough gives his name to the classic midday pub meal.

clue.text: Counters for laboratory vessels

blocks.note: first meaning: sharp replies that counter a remark
second meaning: glass flasks with long bent necks used for distilling

explanation.surface: Workbenches in a chemistry lab where glassware stands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counters' suggests worktops for the glassware; it is the plural noun for comebacks.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means witty comebacks and also the long-necked glass flasks chemists use for distillation.

clue.text: Carroll's joyful blend?

blocks.note: surface reading: a cheerful mixture, perhaps a drink, made by someone called Carroll
setter's reading: Lewis Carroll coined a portmanteau word in Jabberwocky by merging chuckle and snort

explanation.surface: A happy mixture of tea or tobacco sold under the Carroll name.
explanation.walkthrough: A blend is also a portmanteau word; Carroll invented this one in Through the Looking-Glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll formed the word from chuckle and snort to describe a gleeful laugh, which makes it a merged coinage.

clue.text: Wood pigeon in copper's helmet

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper, plus the S of the possessive
a helmet is a kind of hat

explanation.surface: A pigeon perched inside a policeman's helmet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper's helmet' suggests a police officer's headgear; here copper is the metal, CU, and the 's is kept as an S.
explanation.definitionFit: Cushat is a Scottish and northern dialect name for the ring dove, the common large pigeon of woodland.

clue.text: Fair dealer, though shoddy

blocks.note: first meaning: a hawker selling cheap goods at fairs
second meaning: cheap and of poor quality, as an adjective

explanation.surface: An honest trader whose goods are nevertheless badly made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' reads as honest; it is the travelling fair where such pedlars sell their wares.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a travelling pedlar of cheap wares and, as an adjective, describes goods that are inferior.

clue.text: Scriabin's first trio copied, but played badly

indicators.note: the first trio means the opening three letters of the name, taken in order

blocks.note: the opening three letters of the composer's name
to ape is to copy or mimic

explanation.surface: A trio by the Russian composer Scriabin was imitated but badly performed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trio' sounds like a chamber piece; it means three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A poor violinist is said to scrape away at the strings, producing rough, grating sounds.

clue.text: There is water, air-conditioned, in such tanks

indicators.note: conditioning something alters its state, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: aqua is the Latin word for water
the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Fish tanks hold water and are aerated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air-conditioned' reads as one adjective; it splits into the fodder and its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquaria are glass tanks holding water in which fish and plants are kept, the Latin plural of aquarium.

clue.text: Sign of letter missing, with redirected address

blocks.note: first meaning: the punctuation mark showing where a letter has been left out, as in don't
second meaning: in rhetoric, a speech turned away from the audience to address someone absent

explanation.surface: A note about a lost letter that had to be sent on to a new address.
explanation.walkthrough: The postal picture of a missing letter and a forwarding address hides a printed mark and a figure of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names the punctuation mark for an omission and the rhetorical device of turning aside to speak to someone absent.

clue.text: Dismissed after one run and overthrow

blocks.note: R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a run
a batsman who is dismissed is out

explanation.surface: A cricket batsman given out after scoring a single, followed by a wild throw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the word for dismissed behind the run. The cricket picture also makes 'overthrow' look like a fielding error, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rout is a crushing defeat that scatters an enemy, so to overthrow utterly.

clue.text: One may case the joint

blocks.note: surface reading: a burglar inspects premises before a robbery, which is casing the joint
setter's reading: the thin sheet that wraps, or encases, a hand-rolled cannabis joint

explanation.surface: A crook checking out a building before a break-in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case the joint' is gangster slang for reconnoitring a place; read literally it means forming the casing of a cannabis joint.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin rolling sheet wraps the tobacco or cannabis of a hand-rolled smoke, literally forming its casing.

clue.text: Manor-house and land needs me to get organised

indicators.note: getting organised means being put into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: An estate whose owner says it needs someone to sort it out.
explanation.definitionFit: A demesne is the land attached to a manor and kept by the lord for his own use, together with the house.

clue.text: He is abnormally nervous, note, in run-up over Ringway

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from the bottom, so the word runs backwards
in means placed inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
E is one of the musical notes A to G
split as ring and way: a ring is round like the letter O, and a way is a path

explanation.surface: A nervous flyer approaching Ringway, Manchester's airport, in a run-up to landing.
explanation.walkthrough: Ringway was the name of Manchester Airport; here it splits into ring and way. 'Over' puts the first part above the rest in a down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A neuropath is an old term for someone with a nervous disorder, a person suffering from neurosis.

clue.text: Distemper for grim apartment

blocks.note: grim and harsh, as in hard times
pad is slang for a flat or apartment

explanation.surface: Choosing a paint colour to brighten a dismal flat.
explanation.walkthrough: Distemper looks like the wall paint; it is the dog disease.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard pad is a form of canine distemper virus that thickens and hardens the pads of a dog's feet.

clue.text: Everything one stuffed into faded cover for mattress

indicators.note: stuffing something into a case puts it inside, so these words go within the other

blocks.note: passé means past its best, faded
everything is all
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone cramming all their belongings into a worn-out mattress cover.
explanation.definitionFit: A palliasse is a straw-filled sack laid under or used as a mattress, French in origin from paille, straw.

clue.text: Wife-beater appearing for trial after free-for-all

blocks.note: Mr Punch of the Punch and Judy puppet show beats his wife Judy
someone up before the court is appearing for trial

explanation.surface: A violent husband in the dock after a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch and Judy is the traditional British seaside puppet show in which Punch beats Judy. 'After' is not an order signal here: the brawl is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A punch-up is a brawl or fistfight in which everyone joins in, so a free-for-all.

clue.text: Rattle? French article with brass at the bottom

indicators.note: in a down answer the bottom is the end, so this word is placed last, below the other

blocks.note: un is the French for a, the indefinite article
brass is cheek or nerve

explanation.surface: A French brass band with its instruments rattling at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At the bottom' puts the second piece below the first in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To rattle someone is to fluster them and make them lose their composure.

clue.text: Unusual dialect in Dover Castle, say

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the normal order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A strange local accent heard among the visitors at Dover Castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Dover Castle is the medieval fortress above the white cliffs of Kent; 'say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A citadel is a fortress commanding a town, and the castle at Dover is one example of such a stronghold.

clue.text: Set about murder with frying pan

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word sits around the other

blocks.note: taken as written
to murder is to kill

explanation.surface: A killer assaulting a victim with a frying pan.
explanation.definitionFit: A skillet is a small heavy pan with a long handle used for frying food.

clue.text: Gloomy in nasty giant's lair?

indicators.note: in means contained within the following words, so the letters sit inside them

blocks.note: running across the two words
surface padding that completes the picture of a dark den

explanation.surface: A dark cave where an ogre lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lair?' completes the picture and fits the answer, but gives no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stygian means as dark as the river Styx of the Greek underworld, so very dark and dismal.

clue.text: Where witnesses may find the figures on the sheet spectacular?

definitions.text: Where witnesses may find the figures on the sheet spectacular?

blocks.clueFragment: Where witnesses may find the figures on the sheet spectacular?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone giving evidence surprised by numbers on a statement
setter's reading: skaters trace figures on a frozen sheet, and the spectators are the witnesses

explanation.surface: Witnesses in court reading a balance sheet with startling numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: Witnesses means onlookers, figures are skating patterns, and the sheet is a rink.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatrical entertainment performed by skaters on a rink is a spectacle where audiences watch figures traced.

clue.text: Strains without opening locks

indicators.note: without its opening means the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: strains and stresses are pressures

explanation.surface: Pulling at locks that will not open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' suggests things to open; it means hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Tresses are long locks of hair on a woman's head.

clue.text: Cause of the big bang? Origin recently rewritten

indicators.note: something rewritten has been recast in a different form, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A cosmologist's theory of how the universe began has just been revised.
explanation.walkthrough: The Big Bang points to the start of the universe, which 'Origin' backs up; the bang is a literal explosion.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitroglycerine is a powerful unstable liquid explosive, so it can be what causes a loud blast.

clue.text: Network free after midnight

indicators.note: the middle of the night is the centre of that word, so only its central letter is kept

blocks.note: the centre letter of night
to rid someone of something is to free them of it

explanation.surface: Being released from something just after twelve at night.
explanation.walkthrough: Midnight is a crossword convention for the middle letter of night. 'After' would usually put the second piece first; here it is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A grid is a network of crossing lines, as in a power grid or street plan.

clue.text: Reverse for paper following opposition

indicators.note: following means coming behind, so the word before it is placed after the one that follows it

blocks.note: anti means against, in opposition
a thesis is an academic paper

explanation.surface: An academic paper turned around because of objections to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' puts the paper after the opposition.
explanation.definitionFit: An antithesis is the direct opposite of something, so its reverse or converse.

clue.text: Means to break the law

indicators.note: breaking something smashes it apart, so its letters are scattered and reassembled

blocks.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A method of committing a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Means' reads as a verb or a method; it is the noun for money.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of means has money and property, so means in that sense is riches.

clue.text: Without cocaine, having crystalline deposit reduced?

blocks.note: first meaning: snow is slang for cocaine, so lacking it
second meaning, read cryptically: the crystalline deposit is snow, and reduced means there is less of it

explanation.surface: Someone going without drugs, and a report of shrinking frost.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are cryptic: snow is drug slang for cocaine, and the second half splits the word into snow and less.
explanation.definitionFit: The word literally means free of fallen ice flakes, and slang makes those flakes the drug as well.
